grammar.name: Nominalisation for academic register
grammar.rule: This changes verbs or adjectives into nouns — for example, 'reduce' becomes 'reduction'. It creates the formal, impersonal tone used in academic writing.
grammar.formula: verb/adjective -> noun (reduce -> reduction; aware -> awareness)
grammar.example: The steady reduction in resources devoted to government policy and public spending has drawn considerable criticism.
grammar.tip: Do not overuse this. A paragraph full of abstract nouns becomes hard to read, so balance it with clearer, simpler sentences too.

grammar.name: Hedging language for academic caution
grammar.rule: This makes a claim sound less certain and more careful, so you do not overstate your argument.
grammar.formula: It + modal (may/might/could) + be + that... | [adverb] + [modal verb]
grammar.example: It could plausibly be argued that government policy and public spending will require a fundamentally different policy response.
grammar.tip: Avoid strong words like 'always', 'never', or 'proves' unless you are completely sure your evidence supports them.

grammar.name: Ellipsis and substitution for cohesion
grammar.rule: This leaves out or replaces a word that was already used earlier in the sentence. It avoids repeating yourself and helps your writing flow better.

grammar.name: Modal perfect for past speculation

grammar.tip: Choose the modal verb carefully. 'Must have' shows you are almost sure. 'Might have' or 'could have' shows it is just possible.

grammar.tip: Remember: if 'not only' is at the start of the sentence, you must invert the subject and verb. If it is in the middle, you do not.

grammar.name: Inversion after negative adverbials

grammar.name: Inversion in formal conditionals

grammar.tip: Use this pattern only in formal writing. Never use 'if' and the inverted word order together in the same sentence.

grammar.rule: This adds extra, non-essential information by combining a quantity word (like 'many' or 'most') with 'of which' or 'of whom'.

grammar.example: The survey included 1,200 respondents, the majority of whom expressed concern about culture, tradition and identity.
grammar.tip: Always put a comma before this structure, because the extra information is not essential. Never use 'that' instead of 'which' or 'whom' here.

grammar.name: Reduced relative clauses
grammar.rule: This leaves out the relative pronoun (like 'that' or 'which') and the auxiliary verb. It makes the sentence shorter and more academic.
grammar.formula: Noun + [participle clause] (no relative pronoun)
grammar.example: Measures aimed at addressing science, space and innovation require sustained political commitment to succeed.
grammar.tip: You can only shorten a relative clause this way when the pronoun you remove would have been the subject of that clause.

grammar.name: Concession: despite/in spite of + noun/-ing vs. although + clause
grammar.rule: This shows a contrast, but the grammar after it depends on the connector you choose. Use a noun or an -ing phrase after 'despite'/'in spite of'. Use a full clause after 'although'/'even though'.
grammar.formula: Despite/In spite of + noun/-ing, clause. | Although/Even though + clause, clause.
grammar.example: Despite growing awareness of science, space and innovation, meaningful action has been slow to materialise.
grammar.tip: Never put a subject + verb clause right after 'despite' or 'in spite of'. This is one of the most common mistakes at B2 level.

grammar.name: Emphatic do / so...that / such...that
grammar.rule: The word 'do' can add extra stress to a verb, often to correct or contrast something. 'So...that' and 'such...that' make a description stronger and show its result.
grammar.formula: Subject + do/does/did + base verb | so + adj/adv + that-clause | such + (a/an) + adj + noun + that-clause
grammar.example: The evidence on science, space and innovation was so compelling that even sceptical policymakers took notice.
grammar.tip: Use emphatic 'do' only for real contrast or correction. If you use it too often, it loses its effect.

grammar.name: Nominalisation for academic register
grammar.rule: This changes verbs or adjectives into nouns — for example, 'reduce' becomes 'reduction'. It creates the formal, impersonal tone used in academic writing.
grammar.formula: verb/adjective -> noun (reduce -> reduction; aware -> awareness)
grammar.example: The steady reduction in resources devoted to science, space and innovation has drawn considerable criticism.
grammar.tip: Do not overuse this. A paragraph full of abstract nouns becomes hard to read, so balance it with clearer, simpler sentences too.

grammar.name: Hedging language for academic caution
grammar.rule: This makes a claim sound less certain and more careful, so you do not overstate your argument.
grammar.formula: It + modal (may/might/could) + be + that... | [adverb] + [modal verb]
grammar.example: It could plausibly be argued that science, space and innovation will require a fundamentally different policy response.
grammar.tip: Avoid strong words like 'always', 'never', or 'proves' unless you are completely sure your evidence supports them.

grammar.name: Ellipsis and substitution for cohesion
grammar.rule: This leaves out or replaces a word that was already used earlier in the sentence. It avoids repeating yourself and helps your writing flow better.
grammar.formula: ..., and so + auxiliary + subject | auxiliary + not (omitting the repeated verb phrase)
grammar.example: Older generations remain cautious about science, space and innovation, and so, increasingly, do younger ones.
grammar.tip: Only leave out a word when the reader can easily guess it from context. If it is not clear, the sentence becomes confusing instead of smoother.

grammar.name: Proportional comparatives (the...the...)
grammar.rule: This shows a direct link between two things that change together — when one increases or decreases, so does the other.
grammar.formula: The + comparative + clause, the + comparative + clause
grammar.example: The more attention science, space and innovation receives in public debate, the greater the pressure on lawmakers to respond.
grammar.tip: Keep both halves of the sentence grammatically the same. If they do not match, the sentence sounds wrong.
